Slovak opposition party SaS condemned Prime Minister Robert Fico’s government on Friday, Oct. 9, calling the boycott an international disgrace and de facto collaboration with the Kremlin. by Kyiv Post | Oct. 10, 2026, 4:36 pm Flip Share Facebook X (Twitter) LinkedIn Bluesky Email Copy Copied Slovakia’s Prime Minister Robert Fico gestues during a press conference after the V4 + Ireland Prime Ministers’ meeting at Bratislava castle in Slovakia, on Sept. 10, 2026. (Photo by TOMAS BENEDIKOVIC / AFP) Content Share Facebook X (Twitter) LinkedIn Bluesky Email Copy Copied Flip Slovakia was the only EU member state that refused to sign an international declaration committing to the return of Ukrainian children forcibly transferred to Russia , drawing severe condemnation from domestic opposition lawmakers. According to Rapporteur , the “Toronto Pledge,” adopted on Sept. 29 during the multilateral Pathways to Peace conference, was endorsed by the EU and 26 of its 27 member states. Bratislava’s absence from the roster of signatories went largely unnoticed until the Slovak liberal opposition party Freedom and Solidarity (SaS) publicly disclosed the boycott on Friday, Oct. 9. JOIN US ON TELEGRAM Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official . SaS denounced the decision by Slovakian Prime Minister Robert Fico’s left-nationalist government as an “international disgrace” and an act of political “collaboration with the Kremlin .” Advertisement “Whom did this decision serve? Certainly not Ukrainian children, nor Slovakia. Once again, they are helping a man who is subject to an arrest warrant issued by the International Criminal Court,” the SaS leadership said in an official statement, referring to Russian President Vladimir Putin . Fico’s pro-Moscow alignment The decision to break European solidarity on child abductions follows a consistent pattern of foreign policy recalibration by Fico since returning to office in late 2023. Under Fico’s leadership, Bratislava halted state-funded military aid shipments to the Armed Forces of Ukraine, repeatedly obstructed EU sanctions packages aimed at Russia’s fossil fuel sector, and called for the resumption of standard commercial and diplomatic ties with Moscow . Other Topics of Interest Finland Approves 35th Military Aid Package for Ukraine Finnish President Stubb approves the 35th package of aid containing an urgent defense item as total Finnish military aid reaches €3.6 billion. In May, Fico became one of the few European heads of government to travel to Moscow to attend official Victory Day commemorations alongside Putin. Opposition legislators and human rights advocates emphasized that by refusing to sign the declaration, Slovakia aligned itself against universal humanitarian principles. The International Criminal Court in The Hague issued an arrest warrant for Putin and Russian Children’s Rights Commissioner Maria Lvova-Belova in March 2023, charging them with the war crime of unlawful deportation and transfer of children from occupied regions of Ukraine to Russia. Advertisement Slovak civil society organizations echoed the opposition’s criticism, warning that isolating the country from European human rights initiatives damages Bratislava’s credibility within both the EU and NATO . International accountability Slovakia’s refusal to sign the Toronto Pledge comes as international partners expand legal mechanisms to hold perpetrators of child deportations accountable. In Washington, US President Donald Trump signed into law the Lindsey O. Graham Sanctioning Russia and Iran Act of 2026 on Sept. 18. The statute formally established the forcible deportation, unlawful transfer, and unjust detention of Ukrainian children as statutory grounds for mandatory US sanctions, including asset freezes and travel bans against Russian state agencies, regional guardianship boards, and logistics intermediaries. Maksym Maksymov, head of the Ukrainian presidential initiative Bring Kids Back UA, observed that codifying child deportation penalties into binding law ensures that forced removals are treated with the same legal gravity as military offenses. Advertisement Ukrainian officials have documented the unlawful transfer of nearly 20,000 Ukrainian children to Russia and Belarus , where minors are subjected to forced naturalization, ideological indoctrination, and illegal adoptions by Russian families. International human rights monitors have repeatedly warned that Russia’s institutionalized deportation apparatus seeks to systematically erase the national and cultural identity of displaced Ukrainian youth. Photograph: Evan Vucci/Pool Reuters/AP Iran JD Vance letter may offer last chance to avert fresh conflict between US and Iran US vice-president writes to top Iranian security official in sign Washington has not abandoned diplomacy Patrick Wintour Diplomatic editor Thu 29 Oct 2026 15.32 EDT Last modified on Thu 29 Oct 2026 15.57 EDT Share Prefer the Guardian on Google Hopes of averting a major new conflagration between Iran and the US soon after Tuesday’s midterm elections could rest on Iran’s response to a personal letter from the US vice-president, JD Vance , offering to restart diplomacy. The letter, written after predominantly Qatari mediation, was sent to the secretary of Iran’s supreme national security council, Mohsen Rezaei on Sunday. It requires Tehran to agree to make commitments on its nuclear programme at the start of a process that would lead to the opening of the strait of Hormuz within seven days in return for US sanctions relief. A reply is imminent, but Iran is reluctant to give upfront and irreversible commitments on its nuclear programme, such as exporting its stockpile of highly enriched uranium to a third country, if the compensatory US steps, such as lifting sanctions on Iranian oil exports, are reversible. Some form of third-party guarantee that both sides will adhere to their commitments has been discussed, with China often mentioned as the only country of sufficient status to underwrite it. The return of Vance, a sceptic about the war, to the negotiations is significant and a sign the US has not abandoned diplomacy. View image in fullscreen An anti-US mural in Tehran. Photograph: Abedin Taherkenareh/EPA One Democratic senator briefed on the targets the US military had identified in Iran said the plan for a renewed attack was “insane” and would lead to “the likely destruction of our commitment to the rule of law”. In a sign of Iran’s reluctance to meet US demands about sequencing, its chief negotiator, Mohammad Ghalibaf, wrote on X: “Iran’s conditions have been repeatedly and clearly stated to the mediators. The carrot-and-stick approach has no effect on Iran. Progress can only be achieved once Iran’s seven conditions have been agreed upon.” Those conditions include lifting sanctions, ending asset freezes and ending the war on all fronts, a phrase that requires an Israeli ceasefire in Lebanon. The US wants front-loaded, specific commitments about the removal of Iran’s stockpile of highly enriched uranium. Tehran is reluctant to give up its bargaining leverage, and is also resistant to the return of UN nuclear inspectors for fear they might provide the US with intelligence on the whereabouts and state of the stockpile. It has proposed blending the stockpile down so it is no longer usable to make a nuclear weapon. The Vance letter was sent to Rezaei rather than Ghalibaf or the foreign minister, Abbas Araghchi, because Washington judged that decision-making power rests with those closest to the Islamic Revolutionary Guards Corps. In practice, Iran tries to reach decisions through consensus at the highest level of government in a six strong committee. View image in fullscreen The secretary of Iran’s supreme national security council, Mohsen Rezaei. Photograph: Mohammed Salem/Reuters Ghalibaf and Rezaei met the supreme leader, Mojtaba Khamenei, last week to discuss the risk of a new war. Khamenei has said he would like an end to the current state of neither war nor peace. Iran has well-laid plans ready to strike back against US interests in the region, by hitting desalination plants, internet cables and electricity grids across the Gulf. For a third US attack in two years to have any rationale, or prospect of inducing Iran’s capitulation, the plan would require the US, probably in conjunction with a caretaker government in Israel, to mount attacks on previously off-limits targets. Europe would not join the attacks, but the views of the Gulf states, the chief targets of Iran reprisals, would be key. The Connecticut senator Chris Murphy told a briefing at the Middle East Institute: “I did get a fairly detailed conversation about what the war plan would be … I will just say this their plan is insane. It will lead to devastating escalation and the likely destruction of our commitment to the rule of law. “There has been open reporting as to the civilian infrastructure we may be targeting … I think the plan they have developed will lead, in my judgment, to a prolongment [sic] and escalation of this war that will be devastating to our security interest.” Although Tehran trusts Vance marginally more than most White House politicians and envoys, the Iranian high command is still suspicious about his status after he negotiated a 14-point memorandum of understanding which then fell apart when other members of the US administration took charge of its implementation. That led to unilateral US steps to reopen the strait of Hormuz that Iran said contravened the terms of the agreement. Trump also came to detest it because it delayed the start of nuclear talks for as long as 60 days. In an offer made by Tehran on the margins of the UN general assembly recently, it proposed foreshortening the timeframe before nuclear talks started, saying they could start withinsix or seven days of the US restoring the sanctions waiver on its oil exports and the reopening of the strait of Hormuz. https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cmvg.text: Figure caption, Military cemetery decorum: The tradition behind Hegseth's Veterans Day reprimand By Grace Eliza Goodwin Published 11 November 2026 Updated 9 hours ago US Defence Secretary Pete Hegseth has awarded a medal to the guard who reprimanded his group at Arlington National Cemetery. A video of a Veterans Day observance event on Wednesday showed Hegseth, his wife and senior advisers laughing and talking while posing for photos in front of the Tomb of the Unknown Soldier before the guard told them to be quiet. In a statement, the Pentagon later announced that Hegseth had given Specialist Thomas Iglesias a Joint Service Commendation Medal "for the execution of his duties at the Tomb of the Unknown Soldier". Photos shared on the defence secretary's X account showed him presenting the medal to Iglesias. He was accompanied by others whom the Pentagon identified as members of the 3rd US Infantry Regiment, known as the Old Guard, which is responsible for holding vigil over the Tomb of the Unknown Soldier. "We love soldiers. We love standards. Well done, Specialist. Carry on Patriots," the accompanying text on Hegseth's post reads. In the video, the army sentinel on duty later identified as Iglesias can be seen stepping towards Hegseth's group and shouting: "All visitors will maintain an atmosphere of silence and respect at all times." Image source, Secretary of War Pete Hegseth/X Image caption, Hegseth (right) awarding the medal to Specialist Iglesias The Arlington National Cemetery etiquette requests that visitors speak quietly and do not engage in disrespectful or disorderly conduct. The tomb, which is one of the country's most sacred war memorials, marks the final resting place of an unknown soldier who was killed in World War One. Chief Pentagon spokesman Sean Parnell said in a statement: "While commemorating this solemn day, a soldier correctly and respectfully reminded everyone to maintain decorum. "The Secretary and the entire Department have always honoured - and will always honour - the sacrifices our military men and women have made to keep America safe." A service member from the 3rd Infantry Regiment stands watch over the tomb 24 hours a day and has done so since 1948. It is not unusual for them to admonish visitors to the site, according to the BBC's US partner CBS News. They reportedly do so a few times a day. Image source, AFP via Getty Images Image caption, Defence Secretary Pete Hegseth and First Lady Melania Trump bow their heads in prayer during a Veterans Day ceremony at Arlington National Cemetery Earlier, President Donald Trump, Vice-President JD Vance and other top officials attended the annual wreath-laying at the cemetery. During his speech at the ceremony, Trump offered his gratitude to uniformed service members who have fought for the country. He also touted what he sees as his administration's success in the Iran war. Trump also pointed out Hegseth during the ceremony, saying he's done a "fantastic job" as defence secretary. On Tuesday, an effort to impeach the defence secretary under accusations that he waged war on Iran without congressional authorisation failed on Capitol Hill . Hegseth has called the impeachment efforts a "farce" and a "stunt". Figure caption, US Army guard reprimands group that includes US Defence Secretary Pete Hegseth at Arlington National Cemetery.
